title: "275 years of sunspots, overview and detail"
description: "A long time series with a thin overview strip: brush the strip and the main chart zooms to the brushed years. select_interval() and bind_scale(), composed into one widget, plus the range navigator."
categories: [Stories, Interactive, Composition]

```{r}
#| include: false
source("_helper.R")
library(vellumwidget)
```

Astronomers have counted sunspots every month since 1749. Drawn whole, the
record is a row of 25 peaks, the eleven-year solar cycle, and the page width
puts about four years in a pixel. That is enough to see the cycle and not enough
to see one. Overview and detail is the standard fix: a thin strip shows the
whole series, you brush a stretch of it, and the main chart redraws at that
range.

The data is `sunspot.month`, which ships with R: the monthly mean of the
international sunspot number from the Royal Observatory of Belgium (WDC-SILSO),
3,310 months from January 1749 to October 2024.

```{r}
ss <- data.frame(
  date = seq(as.Date("1749-01-15"), by = "month", length.out = length(sunspot.month)),
  n = as.numeric(sunspot.month)
)
# A centred 13-month running mean: the usual way to smooth out the month-to-month noise.
ss$smooth <- as.numeric(stats::filter(ss$n, rep(1 / 13, 13), sides = 2))
```

## Two plots and one selection

The interaction is declared in the spec, not wired up in JavaScript. A free-standing
`select_interval()` defines a brush over `x`. The overview registers it with
`add_selection()`, which makes it the plot you drag on. The detail calls
`bind_scale()` with the same selection, which ties its x range to the brush:
brushing the overview zooms the detail, and clearing the brush (click on empty
space, or press Escape) zooms it back out.

```{r}
brush <- select_interval("window", encodings = "x")

detail <- vplot(ss, width = 9, height = 3.6) |>
  mark_area(x = date, y = n, fill = "#e3cfa4", alpha = 0.8) |>
  mark_line(x = date, y = smooth, color = "#6b4f2c", linewidth = 0.7) |>
  labs(
    title = "Monthly sunspot number, 1749 to 2024",
    subtitle = "Brush the strip below to zoom; the line is a 13-month running mean",
    x = NULL, y = "sunspots"
  ) |>
  theme_minimal() |>
  bind_scale(brush)

overview <- vplot(ss, width = 9, height = 1.1) |>
  mark_area(x = date, y = n, fill = "#b9a888") |>
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) |>
  theme_minimal() |>
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) |>
  add_selection(brush)

sunspots <- concat(detail, overview, ncol = 1, heights = c(3.6, 1.1))
```

`concat()` stacks the two plots into one figure and lines up their panels, so the
strip sits exactly under the chart it controls. The title and subtitle belong to
the detail plot and are drawn above its panel, inside the shared grid. On a static render the selection
does nothing and you get both views at full range:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-alt: "Area chart of monthly sunspot numbers from 1749 to 2024 showing about 25 eleven-year cycles, with a thin overview strip of the same series underneath"
vg(sunspots, "overview-detail", dpi = 120)
```

## The widget

`as_widget()` turns the composition into the interactive version. Drag across a few
decades of the bottom strip and the top chart zooms to them, with its axis
re-ticked for the new range: at fifty years you can count the cycles, at ten you
can see the double peak many of them have, and the dead decades of the Dalton
Minimum around 1800 to 1820 come into focus. Drag the brush to slide the window.

`navigator = navigator_options()` adds the second control, a range navigator
under the widget. It is a miniature of the whole figure with a window on it that
marks what the chart shows. Drag the window to pan, drag either edge to zoom.
It follows the wheel and keyboard zoom too.

```{r}
#| column: page-inset-right
sunspots |>
  as_widget(navigator = navigator_options(height = 48))
```

None of this needs a server. The widget carries both plots, the selection and
the binding in its payload, and the browser enacts them: the brush is
converted to a date range through the overview's own scale, and the detail
redraws at that range. Under Shiny, the same widget reports the brushed range
as `input$<id>_brush`.

For the other ways one view can drive another, see
[linked views with crosstalk](crosstalk.qmd) and
[declarative interactivity](declarative-interactivity.qmd).
